---
title: "Large data and parallel computing"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

## Where the time goes

For each spatial kernel, SIGNAL first computes a **set-up** that is shared by
all genes (the MINQUE weights and the quadratic-form matrices), and then tests
each **gene**. With the default `method = "davies"`, the set-up takes seconds
and nearly all the time is spent on the genes: each needs four
eigendecompositions and six products of n $\times$ n matrices. Run time
therefore grows with the number of genes, the number of kernels (11, or 1 for
large data) and about the cube of the number of cells n.

## Parallel computing

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_test(obj, ncores = 20)                     # all genes, 20 workers
obj <- SIGNAL_test(obj, ncores = 20, parallel = "genes") # the same, explicitly
```

* **`ncores`** defaults to all available cores: the Slurm allocation
  (`SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK`) on a cluster, otherwise all cores of the machine.
* **`parallel = "genes"`**: the kernels are processed one at a time; each
  kernel's set-up is computed once, then the genes are split over `ncores`
  forked workers that share it. Each worker adds only a few n $\times$ n
  matrices of memory.
* **`parallel = "kernels"`**: the kernels are processed in parallel, each
  worker with its own set-up. Useful with `method = "liu"` or
  `"davies_liu"` and few genes, whose set-up is costly, but each worker needs
  about 20–50 n $\times$ n matrices.
* **`parallel = "auto"`** (default) chooses between the two from the numbers
  of kernels, genes and cores, and limits kernel workers to the available
  memory.
* With `verbose = TRUE`, a progress bar shows the genes of each kernel.

The workers are forked processes (`pbmcapply::pbmclapply`). Forking does not
work on Windows, so there SIGNAL runs on one core; use Linux or macOS for
parallel runs.

### BLAS threads

With a multithreaded BLAS (OpenBLAS, MKL), SIGNAL runs each kernel's set-up
with `ncores` BLAS threads and the workers with one thread each, and restores
the previous setting afterwards. Outside the tests, set one thread before
starting R so that the other steps stay within the allocation:

```{bash}
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1
```

## One spatial kernel for large data

With more than 6,000 cells, `SIGNAL_kernel()` builds one Gaussian spatial
kernel instead of the panel of 11, which reduces run time about 11-fold:

```{r}
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj)                         # automatic: 1 kernel above 6,000 cells
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj, approximation = TRUE)   # always 1 kernel
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj, approximation = FALSE)  # always 11 kernels
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj, max_cells = 10000)      # change the threshold
obj <- SIGNAL_kernel(obj, bandwidth = 0.05)       # fix the kernel bandwidth
```

## Memory

One n $\times$ n matrix takes 8 n² bytes:

| Cells | One n $\times$ n matrix | Main process | Each gene worker | 20 workers in total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 8 MB | < 1 GB | < 0.1 GB | < 2 GB |
| 4,410 | 0.16 GB | ~5 GB | ~1.1 GB | ~27 GB |
| 5,520 | 0.24 GB | ~5 GB | ~1.7 GB | ~40 GB |
| 9,244 | 0.68 GB | ~12 GB | ~4.8 GB | ~110 GB |

If workers run out of memory, the operating system stops them and SIGNAL
reports it; use fewer workers (`ncores`) or request more memory.

## Splitting genes over cluster jobs

The genes are tested independently, so a large analysis can be split into
batches, one per task of a Slurm job array, and the result tables combined
afterwards. See the [axolotl brain](Artista.html#run-on-a-cluster-in-batches-of-genes)
example.

## Run time

Measured with `method = "davies"`, one BLAS thread per worker:

| Data | Cells | Kernels | Genes | Cores | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Example data (`SIGNAL_example`) | 400 | 11 | 70 | 20 (Linux) | ~10 s |
| Simulations | 1,000 | 11 | 1,200 | 20 | ~20–40 min |
| Axolotl brain, one batch | 4,410 | 11 | 160 | 20 | ~3 h |
